implementation_notes: The float64 trap: encoding/json decodes every JSON number into float64 by default, silently losing precision for integers outside the 53-bit mantissa range. Fix: create a json.Decoder from an io.Reader, call dec.UseNumber(), and decode into map[string]any. Numbers arrive as json.Number (a string underneath) and are converted to int64 or float64 only when the type of the target field is known — giving the same precision guarantees as a statically-typed struct decode while keeping the document loose.
pitfalls: json.Number is a string in disguise: calling .Float64() or .Int64() on it can still overflow; check the magnitude before converting if the range is bounded.
UseNumber disables automatic integer detection even for fields that are clearly integers in the JSON source — every number must be handled as json.Number or explicitly cast.
json.Decoder reads from an io.Reader, not a string; use strings.NewReader for in-memory JSON.
encoding/json decodes every JSON number into float64, so integers silently lose precision beyond 2^53; use json.Decoder with UseNumber or decode into a struct.
A type assertion without comma-ok panics: d["price"].(float64) on a missing or mistyped key crashes the process.
Maps are not safe for concurrent use: a write through one goroutine while another reads causes a data race (and a fatal error if detected).
